messages.subject: Dividing neuron data frame
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr Jefferis,

I'm currently planning to divide certain neurons into portions whereby each portion of a neuron is arborised in a certain z-coordinate range layer. I was wondering how the package determined EndPoints and BranchPoints. If it is determined by parental connections, would it still be able to find branch and end point when I select only 1 portion of the neuron (e.g. using a dataset with only points contained in the magenta box in the image below)? Furthermore, how would you suggest I approach splitting data of .swc files like this? I hope this email isn't too confusing, thank you for your help!

Best regards,

Ken Nguyen

messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] Dividing neuron data frame
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ken,

You can divide up the neuron with this function

http://natverse.org/nat/reference/subset.neuron.html

I believe the end points and branch points are derived from parental connections and will not change after the division. They can be readily accessed using this:

http://natverse.org/nat/reference/rootpoints.html

best,
arthur

messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] Dividing neuron data frame
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Arthur!

Ken, Arthur is right that subset.neuron should do the trick. Look at the examples in the help page and you should see an example using the coordinates to select points.

After the subset end points should still be fine.

If you need to be more careful about pruning, because processes double back on themselves, then you can also use the spine function to find the longest path through the neuron, optionally setting the argument to start from the root point. Then you can choose points along that spine closest to a five Z position. Then you can prune_distal from the elmr package to select arbours downstream (or upstream of that location). You might get some additional ideas from the neurons as graphs and neurogeometry vignettes of nat.

Best, Greg.

Sent from my iPhone

messages.subject: Re: 3D polygons in R
messages.body_plain:
Dear Daniel,

Thanks for your message. For working with 3D meshes, the tools I use are

* Rvcg R package
* Morpho R package
* meshlab app

I normally use wavefront OBJ format as my interchange format. You can
use the readobj package to import big meshes. Rvcg has the option to
write OBJ meshes (don't use the rgl version – see thread with Dudi
Deutsch for details).

For making meshes from volumetric data, I normally uses Amira. However
you can use Fiji. There is a marching cubes implementation in the 3D
viewer plugin if you make a binary mask of your data. You can then save
to Wavefront OBJ, STL etc. You can follow the first part of the "3D
Content in PDFs" from https://imagej.net/3D_Viewer:_Screencasts. You can
also script this like so: https://imagej.net/3D_Viewer:_Display_a_Stack

To plot surface meshes in R, I either use rgl (e.g. wire3d or mesh3d) or
wrappers of these functions in nat (essentially plot3d.* methods).
Recently we have provided some support in nat using plotly. The pros and
cons of rgl vs plotly are discussed here:

http://natverse.org/nat/articles/plotly.html

Hope this helps. With best wishes,

Greg.

PS I have taken the liberty of ccing this message to the nat-user google
group since the answer may be of interest to others.

--
Gregory Jefferis, PhD
Division of Neurobiology
MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology
Francis Crick Avenue
Cambridge Biomedical Campus
Cambridge, CB2 OQH, UK

http://www2.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/group-leaders/h-to-m/g-jefferis
https://www.zoo.cam.ac.uk/research/groups/connectomics
http://jefferislab.org

messages.subject: Re: About the soma location when using the nblast
messages.subject_clean: About the soma location when using the nblast
messages.body_plain:
Dear MQChen,

Somehow we missed this query last December – apologies.

The current NBLAST implementation is very simple and it does not pay any special attention to soma location – it is just another point. There are various ways that one could try to get round this when the target / query neurons have a soma. For example it would be possible to make a separate probabilistic score for this and add it to the main one.

Best,

Greg.
